summary:
Extremadura stands under Spain's Ley 4/2023 of 28 February 2023, published in the Boletín Oficial del Estado as BOE-A-2023-5366, the law for the real and effective equality of trans people and the guarantee of LGBTI rights. The statute mandates measures across administrative, workplace, health and education fields with public authorities acting within their competences; its education-facing and administrative provisions are implemented by Spain's autonomous communities, and the Extremadura regional government is among the governments that carry them out.

Title II of the law regulates rectification of the registered sex entry by the person's freely expressed will. Under Article 43 any person aged 16 or over may request rectification of the gender mention on their own civil registry entry directly before the Civil Registry, an administrative self-identification route that replaced the former requirement of a gender-dysphoria diagnosis plus two years of medical treatment aligned to the sought marker. The procedure is depathologised: no medical diagnosis and no treatment requirement apply, the former age-majority requirement has been removed, and the corresponding identity documents are adapted after the change. Recognition is possible from age 12 under conditions, a provision that provoked political conflict, and the law regulates consent for medical procedures on minors aged 12 to 16.

Access to sex-separated facilities in Extremadura rests on legal gender self-determination rather than on biological sex, so the gender marker recorded in the civil registry is the operative basis for facility rules. Legal gender change does not require surgery or sterilisation.

Title III provides protection and reparation against LGBTIphobic discrimination and violence. The same statute bans medically unnecessary normalising surgery on intersex children before they can consent, expands assisted reproduction rules, enables parental recognition for unmarried same-sex couples, strengthens sexuality education, and prohibits LGBTI discrimination in healthcare, employment and housing. Same-sex marriage and full adoption rights have been in force in Spain since 2005.

Spain has no free-standing criminal offence of gender-expression-based hate crime: the phrase 'gender expression' appears in no article of the Spanish Criminal Code. The hate-speech aggravating circumstance in Article 22.4 and the penalties of Article 510, one to four years' imprisonment plus a fine of six to twelve months, derive from Organic Law 6/2022, while Ley 4/2023 itself reformed offences against sexual freedom, including Articles 132, 173, 178 to 181 and 189 bis.

Enforcement of the gender-identity aggravation is documented at first-instance level. In July 2026 the Tribunal de Instancia in Vigo applied the transfobia aggravating circumstance for the first time in a misdemeanour case concerning threats sent by WhatsApp to a trans woman, fining the author EUR 300. In a separate case reported on 8 January 2026, a juvenile gang harassed, insulted, beat and filmed a trans person in a park in Valencia to mock them; the only adult defendant received six months' prison and two minors were judged separately.
tangentialFactors:
Human Rights Watch, reporting on 16 February 2023 as the Spanish Congress of Deputies passed the comprehensive LGBTI law known as the 'Trans Law', assessed the reform as upholding European and international standards against abusive, disproportionate requirements for legal gender recognition.

Spain's administrative self-declaration regime places it alongside Argentina, Ireland, Portugal and Uruguay. A 2016 survey of 23 countries ranked Spain the most trans-supportive of the group surveyed and the only country where a majority supported unrestricted legal gender designation change, a dated baseline that predates the 2023 law.

Facility access in Spain is contrasted with the stricter single-sex-space approach being adopted in the United Kingdom on biological-sex lines, where restrictions are applied case by case rather than as a blanket ban.

outOfScopeNotes:
No Extremadura-specific enforcement data, regional decree, or regional facility-access guidance appears in the source inventory; the enforcement evidence available is from first-instance courts in Vigo and Valencia, in other parts of Spain. Whether the transfobia aggravating circumstance has been applied within Extremadura is unresolved and not sourced.

The 2016 23-country survey predates Ley 4/2023 and its ranking should be read as a dated baseline rather than a current measure; no post-2023 comparative survey is available in the inventory.

The inventory does not document how the United Kingdom's biological-sex single-sex-space approach is applied to visitors holding a Spanish or Extremaduran registry marker, so any cross-border comparison of facility rules remains unresolved.
